newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Ailing Yeltsin boosted by Duma approval of budget.
newsitem.headline: Ailing Yeltsin boosted by Duma approval of budget.

text.p: Russia's lower house of parliament on Friday passed the 1997 budget backed by President Boris Yeltsin's government, giving him a much-needed political boost as he recovers from pneumonia.
The State Duma approved the draft budget on its fourth and final reading by 245 votes to 90 against and 17 absentions.
The draft now passes to the upper chamber Federation Council for consideration. It must also be signed by Yeltsin before becoming law.
The president is recovering from double pneumonia, which struck him earlier this month just two weeks after he returned to the Kremlin after undergoing heart surgery.
His press secretary Sergei Yastrzhembsky said Yeltsin was very keen to jump back into Russia's political fray but added he still had not recovered fully.

The Kremlin has not released any photos or videos of the president in more than two weeks, and the first public event Yeltsin was scheduled to attend, a summit of leaders of the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS), was postponed on Friday.
Yastrzhembsky said the 65-year-old president met Kremlin chief of staff Anatoly Chubais at the Gorky-9 residence outside Moscow where he is recovering.

"The president clearly has a huge, burning desire to return as soon as possible to carrying out his duties in full...and it is clear he has retained his characteristic political will," he told a news briefing.

"But on the other hand the president has not fully recovered after his very serious illness, double pneumonia. His physical condition is not good enough to expect him to force his return to the Kremlin," Yastrzhembsky said.
A brief visit to the Kremlin on Wednesday, less than two full days after he left hospital, failed to dispel doubts over Yeltsin's health and his ability to rule.
CIS officials did not cite Yeltsin's health as a reason on Friday for postponing a January 29 Moscow summit of leaders from the former Soviet republics, but they said Yeltsin had agreed to the delay.
Yeltsin's continued absence from the political scene prompted the Duma to debate a motion on Wednesday on trying to oust him, and discussions are set to continue next month.
The president, who was re-elected last July, was out of the Kremlin for most of the second half of 1996 with heart problems, and he had a bypass operation on November 5.
The communists, the largest force in the Duma, had another chance to attack Yeltsin and the government of Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin in the budget debate.
Lawmakers had already approved the bulk of the spending plans but Friday's debate went on late into the night as lawmakers haggled over amendments to the budget.
The draft calls for a 3.5 percent budget deficit, by Russian calculations, on revenues of 434.4 trillion roubles ($77.3 billion) and expenditures of 529.8 trillion roubles.
Also on Friday, U.S. Deputy Secretary of State Strobe Talbott met Chernomyrdin in Moscow to prepare for the prime minister's trip to the United States next month.

NATO sources in Brussels said Talbott had also brought with him new proposals for a deal cutting the huge U.S. advantage in sea-based strategic nuclear missiles as part of efforts to win Russian support for NATO's plans to expand eastwards.
